title: Data Structures & Functions
intro: Lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries, then functions, arguments and functional tools.

sec.s: Python is popular partly because it offers readable syntax and useful built-in tools for organizing data.

b.x: Python is popular partly because it offers readable syntax and useful built-in tools for organizing data. Two foundations of programming are data structures and functions.

A data structure organizes multiple values so a program can store, retrieve, update, and process them. For example, a list can store a student’s marks, a tuple can represent a fixed coordinate, a set can keep unique course names, and a dictionary can connect a student’s roll number to a record.
A function is a reusable block of code that performs a particular task. Instead of copying the same calculation throughout a program, we can define it once and call it whenever needed.
These concepts appear in many areas

x: Websites use lists and dictionaries to display products and represent API responses.
Data-analysis programs use collections to clean, filter, group, and summarize records.
Backend services use functions to validate requests and apply business rules.
Machine-learning pipelines transform and filter datasets before training.
Database results are often represented in Python as lists of dictionaries or other structured objects.

b.x: The goal is not simply to memorize methods. You should understand what each structure is designed for, what its limitations are, and how to select the right tool for a problem. Examples below use Python 3.

b.x: A data structure defines how values are organized and accessed. Python’s common built-in collection types are lists, tuples, sets, and dictionaries.

b.x: A sequence is an ordered collection whose elements have positions. Lists, tuples, and strings are sequences. Python uses zero-based indexing: the first item has index 0, the second has index 1, and so on. Negative indexes count from the end.
Many sequences support concatenation and repetition
Not every sequence supports mutation. Lists are mutable, while tuples and strings are immutable.

sec.s: A list stores multiple values in a particular order.

b.x: A list stores multiple values in a particular order. Lists are flexible and frequently used in Python.
Creating lists
Lists can contain different data types, but collections with a consistent meaning are often easier to work with.
Accessing and changing values
A loop processes each item
Use enumerate() when both index and value are needed:
Adding elements

x: append(value) adds one object to the end.
extend(iterable) adds each item from an iterable.
insert(index, value) inserts before the specified position.

b.x: Important distinction: append([4, 5]) adds the entire list as one nested item. extend([4, 5]) adds 4 and 5 separately.
Removing elements

x: remove(value) removes the first matching value.
pop() removes and returns the last item.
pop(index) removes and returns an item at an index.
del deletes an item or slice.

b.x: remove() raises ValueError when the value is absent. pop() raises IndexError if the list is empty or the index is invalid. Handle these cases when they are possible.
Searching and counting
index() returns the first matching position. It raises ValueError if no match exists.
Sorting and reversing
sort() changes the existing list and returns None. sorted() creates a new sorted list:
A common error is values = values.sort(). After this assignment, values becomes None. Use values.sort() or values = sorted(values).
Copying lists
Assignment does not create an independent copy:
Both names refer to the same list. Use copy() or a slice for a shallow copy:

A shallow copy does not recursively copy nested objects. If two copied outer lists contain the same inner list, modifying that inner list can be visible through both copies. copy.deepcopy() can be useful when a fully independent nested copy is required.
Useful built-in functions

x: print(any(mark >= 90 for mark in marks)) # True
print(all(mark >= 40 for mark in marks)) # True

b.x: any() is true when at least one item is truthy. all() is true when every item is truthy; notably, all([]) is True.

sec.s: A tuple is an ordered sequence that cannot have its element references reassigned after creation.

b.x: A tuple is an ordered sequence that cannot have its element references reassigned after creation. It is useful for grouping values that form a fixed record.
The comma makes a one-item tuple
Parentheses can group expressions without creating tuples, so the comma is important.
Tuples support indexing, slicing, iteration, membership checks, len(), and common sequence operations:
This is invalid because tuple positions cannot be reassigned:
Immutability is shallow. A tuple can contain a mutable list:
The tuple’s reference to the list did not change, but the list itself did.
Tuple methods: - count(value) counts occurrences. - index(value) finds the first matching position.
Tuple unpacking
The number of variables normally matches the number of values. Extended unpacking captures multiple items:
Swapping variables can be written elegantly

Tuples are useful for fixed records, returning multiple results from a function, and creating composite dictionary keys when every element is hashable. They are not automatically better or safer in every situation; choose them when their meaning fits the problem.

sec.s: A set stores unique hashable elements.

b.x: A set stores unique hashable elements. It is useful for removing duplicates, membership tests, and mathematical set operations.
{} creates an empty dictionary, not an empty set. Use set() for an empty set.
Sets do not provide ordinary positional indexing. Do not depend on their displayed order. Set elements must be hashable; lists and dictionaries cannot be elements.
Adding and removing

x: remove(x) removes an element or raises KeyError.
discard(x) removes it if present and otherwise does nothing.
pop() removes and returns an arbitrary element.

b.x: Use discard() when a missing element is acceptable; use remove() when absence should be treated as an error.
Membership and mathematical operations

x: print(A - B) # difference: in A but not B
print(A ^ B) # symmetric difference: in either, but not both

b.x: Subset and superset
Set comprehension

x: squares = {n * n for n in range(1, 6)}

b.x: The result retains only unique values. Set membership is generally efficient on average, but sets have extra memory overhead and remove duplicate information.

sec.s: Quick reference

b.x: Use a list when order matters, duplicates are meaningful, or you need indexing and modification. Example: marks in the order they were recorded.
Use a tuple when values form a fixed ordered record. Example: a coordinate (x, y) or a function returning (minimum, maximum).
Use a set when only uniqueness matters, membership checks are frequent, or you need union and intersection. Example: unique registered course codes.

A set is not a replacement for every list. Converting a list to a set loses duplicate counts and does not preserve list-style positional behavior. If original order matters while removing duplicates, use a separate seen set and a result list.

sec.s: A mapping connects keys to values.

b.x: A mapping connects keys to values. Python’s built-in mapping type is dict, commonly called a dictionary. Rather than requesting an item by its position, you retrieve a value using a meaningful key.
Keys are unique. Assigning to an existing key updates its value:
A dictionary can contain lists, tuples, booleans, numbers, other dictionaries, and None.
Keys must be hashable. Strings, integers, and suitable tuples are common keys. Lists and dictionaries cannot be keys because they are mutable and unhashable.
Missing keys and get()
Square-bracket access raises KeyError if the key is absent:
Use get() when the key may not exist:
get() does not add the missing key. To test key membership:
For a dictionary, in checks keys by default, not values:

x: print("Asha" in student)        # False unless Asha is a key

b.x: Iterating through dictionaries

Modern Python dictionaries preserve insertion order. Updating an existing key does not normally move it to the end; adding a new key places it at the end. For positional sequence operations, a list is still the more suitable structure.

sec.s: A function is a reusable block of code.

b.x: A function is a reusable block of code. It helps prevent repetition and gives a meaningful name to an operation.
def begins the definition, the function name identifies it, parentheses contain parameters, and indentation marks the body. Defining a function does not run its body; calling it does.
A parameter is a name in a function definition. An argument is a value supplied when calling the function.
Here name is a parameter and "Asha" is the argument.
Return versus print
print() displays information. return sends a value back to the caller.
A function without an explicit return statement returns None. A returned value can be saved, compared, passed into another function, or used in calculations.
Functions can return lists, dictionaries, tuples, booleans, and other objects:

x: "average": sum(numbers) / len(numbers) if numbers else None

b.x: Returning multiple values usually returns a tuple:
Handle invalid input deliberately. For division, a function might raise a clear exception:

x: raise ValueError("The divisor cannot be zero.")

built-in names such as len() and sum().

b.x: Local variables
total is local to calculate(). Parameters are also local names.
Global variables
The function can read the global rate, but relying on too much global state can make code harder to test. Passing dependencies as parameters is often clearer.
To reassign a global variable inside a function, use global:
This is valid, but global mutation should be used thoughtfully.
Enclosing scope and nonlocal
nonlocal refers to a name in an enclosing function. It is not the same as global.

A subtle rule: if a name is assigned anywhere in a function body, Python normally treats it as local unless declared global or nonlocal. Reading it before the local assignment may raise UnboundLocalError.
Avoid naming variables list, len, or sum, because that hides built-in names and can cause confusing errors.

sec.s: Keyword arguments can make calls easier to read.

b.x: Arguments provide data to functions.
Positional arguments
Values are matched by position
The order matters.
Keyword arguments
Values are matched by parameter name
Keyword arguments can make calls easier to read. Positional arguments must appear before keyword arguments in a normal call:
This is invalid because a positional argument follows a keyword argument: describe(name="Asha", 19, course="BCA")
Python can declare positional-only and keyword-only parameters:

The slash means a must be supplied positionally. The asterisk means c must be supplied by keyword. These are useful for designing APIs, though ordinary positional and keyword arguments are enough for many beginner programs.

sec.s: A default argument supplies a value when the caller omits the parameter:

b.x: A default argument supplies a value when the caller omits the parameter:
Parameters with defaults normally follow required parameters.
The mutable default argument trap
Avoid this pattern
The same list is reused between calls because the default expression is evaluated once when the function is defined.
Use None instead
Each call that omits items gets a new list. Defaults should be predictable and documented.

sec.s: Sometimes a function should accept an unknown number of positional arguments.

b.x: Sometimes a function should accept an unknown number of positional arguments. *args gathers extra positional arguments into a tuple.
The name args is conventional; the asterisk performs the gathering.
For extra keyword arguments, use **kwargs, which gathers them into a dictionary:
A function can combine these forms
Here title receives a regular argument, values gathers extra positional values, separator is keyword-only, and details gathers remaining keyword arguments.
Unpacking arguments

* unpacks an iterable into positional arguments. ** unpacks a mapping into keyword arguments whose keys match parameter names. Use variable-length arguments when flexibility is useful, not simply to make every function accept arbitrary inputs.

sec.s: Functional programming is a style that emphasizes functions as values and transformations of data.

b.x: Functional programming is a style that emphasizes functions as values and transformations of data. Python supports this style alongside procedural and object-oriented programming.
Useful ideas include

x: Returning functions or storing them in variables.

b.x: A pure-style function
It does not change external state and returns the same result for the same input.
A function that modifies a global counter has a side effect:
Pure functions are often easier to test, but real programs still need side effects such as reading files, saving to databases, or sending network requests.
Python’s functional tools include lambda, map(), filter(), and functools.reduce(). List comprehensions and generator expressions are also valuable tools for transforming data.

sec.s: map() applies a function to each item from an iterable.

b.x: map() applies a function to each item from an iterable. Its common form is map(function, iterable).
In Python 3, map() returns an iterator, not a list. Convert it to a list if you need to display or store all results immediately.
Equivalent list comprehension
Use an existing function
Transform strings
map() can accept multiple iterables when the function takes multiple arguments:

x: print(list(map(lambda x, y: x + y, a, b)))

b.x: With multiple iterables, processing stops when the shortest iterable is exhausted.
Iterators are consumed
If you need the values repeatedly, store them in a list or create a new iterator. Use map() when it reads clearly; a comprehension is often more natural for a simple transformation.

sec.s: filter() selects items for which a function returns a truthy result.

b.x: filter() selects items for which a function returns a truthy result. The function is often called a predicate.
Equivalent comprehension

x: evens = [number for number in numbers if number % 2 == 0]

b.x: A named predicate can make the condition clearer:
If the function is None, filter() keeps truthy elements:
Be careful: this removes all falsy values, including zero, empty strings, False, and None. That may not match the intended rule.
Filtering dictionary records often reads clearly as a dictionary or list comprehension. Choose the form that best communicates the condition.

sec.s: reduce() combines iterable items cumulatively using a function that accepts two arguments.

b.x: reduce() combines iterable items cumulatively using a function that accepts two arguments. It is imported from functools.

x: total = reduce(lambda accumulated, number: accumulated + number, numbers)

b.x: Conceptually: 1. Combine 1 and 2 to get 3. 2. Combine 3 with the next item, 3, to get 6. 3. Combine 6 with 4 to get 10.
An initial value can be supplied

x: product = reduce(lambda acc, n: acc * n, [1, 2, 3, 4], 1)

b.x: The initial value is the starting accumulator. It also defines the result for an empty iterable:

x: total = reduce(lambda a, b: a + b, [], 0)

b.x: Without an initial value, reduce() raises TypeError on an empty iterable. For sums, use sum(). For products, math.prod() is often clearer. reduce() is best when a cumulative combination is genuinely appropriate and no clearer built-in expresses the task.

x: lambda best, current: best if len(best) >= len(current) else current,

b.x: Here, max(words, key=len) is usually clearer. Do not use reduce() just to make code look advanced; readability matters more than compactness.

sec.s: Suppose we need the sum of the squares of even numbers from 1 to 10:

b.x: Suppose we need the sum of the squares of even numbers from 1 to 10:

x: squares = map(lambda n: n * n, evens)
total = reduce(lambda a, b: a + b, squares, 0)

b.x: The stages are: 1. filter() keeps 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10. 2. map() turns them into 4, 16, 36, 64, and 100. 3. reduce() adds them to 220.
A clearer alternative is often

x: total = sum(n * n for n in range(1, 11) if n % 2 == 0)

b.x: Both demonstrate a useful data-processing pipeline

x: Transform: What value should be calculated or normalized?
Aggregate: What single summary should be produced?

b.x: This mental model is useful in data cleaning, analytics, and machine-learning preparation.

For simple transformations, comprehensions are often clearer than map() or filter(). Use a named function when the operation has a meaningful reusable purpose. Use iterator-based approaches when processing a stream without building a large list is helpful.

sec.s: Pitfalls and fixes

x: Assigning the result of sort(). sort() returns None; use it in place or use sorted().
Forgetting zero-based indexing. Index 1 is the second item.
Using an invalid index. Direct indexing can raise IndexError.
Creating a one-item tuple without a comma. Use (5,).
Using {} for an empty set. It creates a dictionary; use set().
Putting a list in a set. Lists are unhashable; use suitable tuples when appropriate.
Accessing a missing dictionary key. Use get(), test membership, or handle KeyError.
Expecting print() to return a value. It returns None; use return for reusable results.
Using a mutable default argument. Use None and create a new list or dictionary inside the function.
Forgetting to import reduce. Use from functools import reduce.
Expecting map() or filter() to return lists. Convert the iterator with list() when necessary.
Reusing an exhausted iterator. Create a new iterator or save results.
Changing a collection while iterating over it. Iterate over a copy or build a new collection.
Overcomplicating a lambda. Use def for substantial logic.
Shadowing built-ins. Avoid names such as list, sum, or len for your variables.

b.x: Debugging routine: 1. Read the last line of the traceback for the error type and message. 2. Find the exact line that failed. 3. Inspect values and types with print(type(value), value). 4. Reduce the program to a small example. 5. Test empty inputs, missing keys, duplicate data, zero, and invalid types. 6. Fix the incorrect assumption instead of blindly suppressing the error.

sec.s: Time complexity describes how work grows with input size.

b.x: Time complexity describes how work grows with input size. Big O notation expresses the general growth pattern. These are common average-case expectations for Python’s built-in collections, not absolute guarantees.

x: List append at the end: amortized O(1).
Inserting or deleting near the start of a list: O(n), because elements may shift.
Set membership: average O(1), though worst-case behavior can be worse.
Dictionary lookup: average O(1), though worst-case behavior can be worse.
Sorting a list: typically O(n log n).

b.x: Here n is the number of items. O(1) means constant expected work with respect to collection size; O(n) means work grows approximately in proportion to the number of items.

If you repeatedly check whether values exist in a large list, a set may be faster on average for membership tests, but converting to a set has a cost and removes duplicate information. Think about the whole task.

Lists, sets, and dictionaries have different memory overheads. For small collections, clarity is usually more important than micro-optimization. Do not assume map() is always faster than a comprehension; performance depends on the operation, Python version, data size, and surrounding work. Write readable code first and measure if performance becomes a real concern.

b.x: Summary

Lists are ordered and mutable. They support indexing, slicing, duplicates, and methods such as append(), extend(), remove(), pop(), and sort(). List comprehensions create lists by transforming and optionally filtering items.
Tuples are ordered and immutable at the sequence level. They are useful for fixed groups of values, unpacking, and returning multiple results. A one-item tuple requires a comma.

Sets store unique hashable values. They support membership checks and mathematical operations such as union, intersection, difference, and symmetric difference. They do not provide ordinary positional indexing.

Dictionaries map unique hashable keys to values. keys(), values(), and items() support iteration. get() is useful for optional keys, update() merges entries, and dictionary comprehensions create mappings.

Functions encapsulate reusable tasks. Parameters are names in definitions; arguments are values supplied in calls. return sends a result to the caller, while print() displays output. Scope determines where names are accessible.

Default arguments provide optional values. Keyword arguments make calls explicit. *args gathers extra positional arguments into a tuple, while **kwargs gathers extra keyword arguments into a dictionary. Avoid mutable default values unless shared state is intentional.

Functional techniques treat functions as values and emphasize transformations. Lambda creates small anonymous functions, map() transforms items, filter() selects items, and functools.reduce() combines items cumulatively. Comprehensions and built-ins are often the clearest choice for simple tasks.
